projects.title: UWASIC
projects.subtitle: Digital design, from RTL to layout.
projects.summary: Designing functional-unit RTL for Waterloo’s ray-tracing ASIC, building on a completed SPI/PWM onboarding project.

cover.alt: Top-down view of the chip layout: rows of standard cells crossed by vertical power straps, with the routed SPI and PWM logic concentrated in the upper half.
cover.caption: GDS layout of my SPI/PWM onboarding design, shown in a 3D layout viewer.

overview: I’m an RTL design member of UWASIC, the University of Waterloo’s chip design team. My current work is functional-unit RTL for a ray-tracing ASIC, collaborating with the verification team toward passing functional tests and a lint-clean RTL-to-GDS flow.

Before that work, I completed a digital-design onboarding project: a Verilog SPI Mode 0 peripheral with register-controlled outputs and PWM. That project connected RTL implementation, automated verification, and physical-layout generation.

sections.title: The peripheral
body: The onboarding peripheral has five registers and sixteen outputs. I implemented SPI Mode 0 communication and two-stage clock-domain crossing to move signals between clock domains.
bullets: Verilog RTL for the SPI peripheral and output controls.
Register interface for configuring peripheral behavior.
Two-stage CDC for signals crossing clock domains.

sections.title: Verification & tooling
body: I wrote Python/cocotb tests for 3 kHz PWM, checking 0%, 50%, and 100% duty cycles as well as output-enable behavior. I configured Tiny Tapeout and GitHub Actions to run simulation tests and generate GDS layout files.

sections.title: Current work
body: I’m now applying that foundation to functional-unit RTL for UWASIC’s ray-tracing ASIC. This is ongoing team work; the completed peripheral and its verification flow are the onboarding portion of the project.

outcome: Completed the SPI/PWM onboarding project with automated simulation tests and GDS generation. The next stage is continuing functional-unit design and verification with the UWASIC team.

projects.title: SignEd
projects.subtitle: A more hands-on way to learn ASL.
projects.summary: An interactive ASL learning website that connects live hand-pose recognition with guided lessons.

cover.alt: The five-person SignEd team standing in front of a projected slide that reads “1st Place Winner, Beginner Tier, $650, SignEd”, most of them making the ASL “I love you” sign.
cover.caption: Our team after SignEd won first place in the Beginner Track at Hack the Bias.

overview: SignEd is an ASL learning website built for Hack the Bias. As the team’s sole programmer, I developed the application using Python, Flask, JavaScript, and HTML/CSS, connecting computer vision to an interactive learning experience.

sections.title: Recognizing a sign
body: MediaPipe and OpenCV provide the hand-tracking pipeline. I normalized 21 three-dimensional hand landmarks by wrist position and hand size, then used distance-weighted K-nearest neighbors to recognize ASL poses.

sections.title: Connecting recognition to learning
body: Live recognition feedback is connected to guided lessons. A learner unlocks progression after holding the correct sign for three seconds, connecting the recognition result to a clear practice goal.

sections.title: My contribution
bullets: Implemented the Python/Flask application and the browser interface.
Built the hand-landmark normalization and pose-classification pipeline.
Connected live feedback to lesson progression.

outcome: SignEd won the Beginner Track at Hack the Bias. The project brought together computer vision, a web interface, and guided practice in one ASL learning experience.

projects.title: VEX Robotics
projects.subtitle: Build. Test. Tune. Compete.
projects.role: Built the intake, flywheel & catapult; programmed autonomous
projects.summary: A VEX competition robot: a flywheel design that qualified our team for the 2023 World Championship, then a catapult rebuild.

cover.alt: Team 2088D’s first robot on the floor: an aluminum VEX frame on omni wheels with a disc intake, a flywheel, and a red 2088D license plate.
cover.caption: Design 1: the flywheel robot that qualified our team for Worlds.

overview: I competed in VEX robotics on team 2088D. Over the 2022–23 season we built two versions of our robot: a flywheel design that qualified us for the World Championship, and a catapult rebuild. I built the intake, the flywheel, and the catapult, and I programmed the autonomous routines.

sections.title: Design 1: the flywheel robot
body: Our first robot collected discs with an intake and launched them with a spinning flywheel. I built both, then tuned the flywheel speed and the intake spacing to make shots more consistent and reduce jams. This is the robot that placed second in Alberta Provincial Robot Skills and qualified us for Worlds.

sections.title: Autonomous routines
body: I programmed the robot’s autonomous routines: the code that drives it on its own at the start of each match and in programming skills runs.

sections.title: Design 2: the catapult rebuild
body: Even after tuning, the flywheel wasn’t as reliable as we wanted. After qualifying for Worlds, we rebuilt the robot around a catapult, which launches a whole stack of discs in one motion. I built the catapult.

images.alt: The rebuilt robot on a workbench, nearly finished: an aluminum frame on omni wheels with a geared catapult arm held back by rubber bands, and a practice field behind it.
images.caption: The catapult rebuild, nearly finished.

images.alt: Video of the catapult launching a stack of three discs into the goal.
images.caption: The catapult launching three discs into the goal.

outcome: The flywheel robot placed second in Alberta Provincial Robot Skills and qualified our team for the VEX Robotics World Championship, where we competed in Dallas in 2023. Its reliability problems led to the catapult rebuild.

projects.title: C++ Ray Tracer
projects.subtitle: Following light, one ray at a time.
projects.summary: A C++ path tracer built up in stages, from a first ray–sphere hit test to Monte Carlo diffuse lighting.

cover.alt: The ray tracer’s final render: a matte grey sphere resting on curved grey ground under a blue sky, with soft shading and a fine grain of sampling noise.
cover.caption: The final render: diffuse lighting averaged over many random samples per pixel.

overview: I built a path tracer from scratch in C++, following the approach in Ray Tracing in One Weekend. It sends rays from the camera through each pixel into the scene and works out what colour each one should be.

I built it up in four stages, each adding one idea and checked with a render before moving on: first finding what a ray hits, then the surface’s orientation, then a sky, and finally how light bounces.

sections.title: Stage 1: rays and a sphere
body: Each ray is a parametric line, P(t) = O + t·d. Substituting it into the sphere’s equation gives a quadratic in t: the discriminant says whether the ray misses, grazes, or hits the sphere, and the smallest positive root is the point the camera sees.
For the first render, rays that hit the sphere were coloured red and rays that missed were black.

images.alt: A flat red circle on a black background.
images.caption: Stage 1: the hit test. Red where a ray hits the sphere, black where it misses.

sections.title: Stage 2: surface normals
body: To make the sphere look three-dimensional, each hit point needs a surface normal. For a sphere it is the direction from the centre to the hit point, (P − C) / R. Before adding any lighting, I checked the normals visually by mapping their x, y, and z components from [−1, 1] to red, green, and blue.

images.alt: A sphere on a black background, shaded in a smooth gradient of cyan, blue, purple, and pink by the direction its surface faces.
images.caption: Stage 2: each pixel coloured by the direction of the surface normal.

sections.title: Stage 3: a sky
body: Next, I replaced the black background with a sky. Each ray that misses takes its colour from a linear blend between white and blue, based on how far up it points.

images.alt: The normal-coloured sphere against a sky that fades from light blue at the top to near-white at the bottom.
images.caption: Stage 3: a gradient sky behind the sphere.

sections.title: Stage 4: diffuse light and random sampling
body: Finally, I made the surfaces matte. When a ray hits one, it bounces off in a random direction and picks up colour from wherever it goes next. To choose the direction, I pick random points in a cube and keep the first one that falls inside a unit sphere. This is Monte Carlo path tracing.

With one random sample per pixel, the image was very noisy. Averaging many samples per pixel smooths out both the noise and the jagged edges, because the average converges to the true lighting as the number of samples grows. The cost is time: more samples meant much longer renders. The result is at the top of this page.

outcome: The finished ray tracer turns vectors, quadratic equations, and random sampling into soft, realistic shading. It is limited to matte spheres, with no specular reflections, transparency, or other shapes yet. Natural next steps are ray–plane intersections and triangle meshes, which would allow more complex scenes.

projects.title: Calgary Ace Learning Center
projects.subtitle: Learning together. Giving back.
projects.summary: A student-run nonprofit bringing together tutoring, volunteer organizing, and fundraising for children’s healthcare.

highlights.label: Raised for the Alberta Children’s Hospital Foundation

overview: I co-founded Calgary Ace Learning Center, a student-run nonprofit. My work focuses on tutoring, organizing, and fundraising: contributing time to help students learn while supporting a cause beyond the classroom.

sections.title: Teaching & volunteering
body: I have contributed more than 400 volunteer hours through tutoring and organizing. Teaching is a central part of my involvement, alongside the work needed to help a student-run organization operate.

sections.title: Fundraising for children’s healthcare
body: I led fundraising that raised more than $5,000 for the Alberta Children’s Hospital Foundation. This work connected our student-led organization with a broader community purpose.

sections.title: Building the organization
body: As a co-founder, I contribute to both the educational work and the organization behind it. I also built its WordPress website to support its online presence.

outcome: An ongoing commitment to education and community service, with more than 400 volunteer hours contributed and $5,000+ raised for the Alberta Children’s Hospital Foundation.
